- When does an item move from "live storage" into "server-side archive" (i.e., cold storage, lower-cost tier)? Is this based on inactivity, a TTL, or manual lifecycle jobs?
- If a customer requests an immediate purge for a set of sessions (DSAR / account deletion), which copies are removed (hot caches, archive, backups)? How far back does the purge pipeline reach?
- Do short-lived items like streaming token fragments and KV-cache entries get archived at all? If yes, what are typical retention horizons?

Asha — thanks for the clear list. Below is a concise, actionable breakdown you can paste into the questionnaire. I attached a compact retention matrix (retention_matrix_v2.pdf) and our internal deletion runbook (redacted) for your review.

Quick answers (high level):

1) Server-side archive vs live storage:
- Live/hot storage: the recent request/response objects and active session KV cache live in our hot cluster for the duration of a session and for the short default capture horizon.
- Archive (cold): objects older than the account's capture horizon (default 45 days for generated outputs + 45 days for full request/response artifacts) are moved by lifecycle jobs to cold storage. Movement is TTL-driven (based on last access or session end) and executed by automated lifecycle jobs — customers with Dedicated/Private can set custom TTLs.

2) Customer-initiated purge (DSAR / account deletion):
- Trigger: when a customer submits a purge request via Support or the Self-Serve Data controls, it initiates our deletion pipeline.
- Scope: the pipeline removes records from hot storage, then schedules deletion from cold storage and any nearline backups. We also emit deletion events (audit log) that we can deliver to you.
- Timing: hot items are typically flagged for immediate deletion; full removal from archived backups can take up to the backup retention cycle (we accelerate this where the customer has a contractual requirement).
- Exceptions: legal holds and regulatory export freezes can delay purge. We will always surface such exceptions early in the process.

3) Streaming fragments, KV cache, prefix caches:
- Ephemeral KV / streaming fragments: these are session-scoped and are not promoted to archive by default. They are kept in-memory / local SSD with short TTLs (default 24h) and garbage-collected unless the customer opts into longer capture (for debugging or transcript storage).
- Prefix / KV cache used for caching prompts: unless configured to persist, cache entries are temporary and not kept in cold storage. If a customer requests persistence (e.g., transcript retention), those objects are explicitly promoted and then follow normal TTL/archival rules.

4) What "archived" means for you:
- Archived = moved to a lower-cost blob/nearline tier and subject to a separate retention lifecycle. Objects in archive are still deletable by the purge pipeline, but propagation to all copies (including offsite backups) is asynchronous.

5) Auditing and proof of deletion:
- We can provide a deletion event log (exportable CSV) that shows the object IDs, timestamps, and pipeline status. For enterprise customers we can also provide a signed attestation of deletion.

Practical note: if BrightBank needs guaranteed same-day removal from all backups we should capture that as an SLA addendum (that accelerates backup purge windows).

Asha — adding two concrete examples to help your risk team: 

Example 1 — Real-time chat with ephemeral sessions:
- User messages are held in hot storage for the session + 24h by default. If no retention override is set, those objects are tombstoned and then moved to archive after 45 days. Purge request during the first 24h removes from hot immediately; purge after archival initiates the archive/backups pipeline.

Example 2 — Batch ingestion where customer elects transcript retention:
- Customer enables "persist transcripts" flag: transcript artifacts are written to customer-owned S3 (if configured) and also to Redwood's archive for search/observability. These persist according to the account TTL until deleted by customer action or TTL expiry.

How to request immediate purge (recommended path):
1) Open a Support ticket with the subject "Data Purge: <account-id>" (include timestamps & object ids if known).
2) For DSARs: use the DSAR portal link in the customer console or email support@redwood.com with the DSAR form attached.
3) We notify you when objects are queued for deletion and when propagation to backups begins (audit events).

Asha — we'll include the support ticket template and the DSAR link in the retention_matrix_v2.pdf for you.
